issues.legal_issue: Where an impartible estate devolves on the nearest male relative and rival claimants are equally related to the common ancestor, the senior line prevails under the rule of lineal primogeniture.
material_facts: The estate was impartible and, in the absence of a legitimate or adopted son, devolved on the nearest male relative.
The rival claimants were equally removed from the common ancestor, but one descended from the elder branch.
The governing custom applied the rule of lineal primogeniture.
issues.conclusion: The claimant from the senior line was the nearest male relative entitled to succeed; being older in age alone did not give the rival claimant priority.
issues.legal_principle: Succession to an impartible estate is governed by the rules applicable to partible property, subject to the special rule selecting a single heir. The class of heirs entitled under the general law must first be ascertained; where claimants are of the same class and no special custom provides otherwise, primogeniture selects the heir. The Court relied on Subramanya Pandya Chokka Talawar v. Siva Subramanya Pillai, I.L.R. 17 Mad. 316, at p. 325.

rule.if: impartible_estate_succession_dispute and holder_left_no_son_or_adopted_son and claimants_equally_related and one_claimant_descends_from_senior_line

predicates.impartible_estate_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns succession to an estate held as impartible.
predicates.holder_left_no_son_or_adopted_son: The holder died without a legitimate or adopted son.
predicates.claimants_equally_related: The competing claimants were equally removed from the common ancestor under the applicable rules of succession.
predicates.one_claimant_descends_from_senior_line: One competing claimant descended from the senior line of the family.

issues.definition: When an impartible-estate succession dispute arises without a surviving legitimate or adopted son, and equally related claimants include one from the senior line, the senior-line claimant succeeds.

issues.legal_issue: Governmental powers to impose conditions on an impartible estate and remove an unfit holder do not by themselves reduce the holder’s interest to a life interest.
material_facts: The estate had been confirmed in favour of an ancestor under a grant subject to conditions concerning loyalty, administration, and improvement of the estate.
The grant authorized governmental action against an unfit holder and provided for succession to the next heir if a holder was removed.
Successions of successive holders were recognized without evidence of fresh grants being issued each time.
issues.conclusion: The governmental powers and conditions were restrictions on the estate, but did not make the holder a mere life tenant.
issues.legal_principle: The grant and the recorded terms of tenure must be read as a whole. A power to remove a holder for misconduct or failure to meet conditions does not convert the holder’s interest into a life interest; succession remains according to the family custom, and removal operates as though the holder had died.

rule.if: impartible_estate_tenure_dispute and grant_subject_to_governance_conditions and government_can_remove_unfit_holder and successions_recognized_without_fresh_grants

predicates.impartible_estate_tenure_dispute: The proceeding concerns the nature of the holder’s interest in an impartible estate.
predicates.grant_subject_to_governance_conditions: The estate was held subject to conditions concerning matters such as loyalty, administration, or improvement.
predicates.government_can_remove_unfit_holder: The government had authority to remove a holder who failed to meet the conditions or was otherwise unfit.
predicates.successions_recognized_without_fresh_gra: Successions to the estate were recognized without evidence that a new grant was made to each successor.

issues.definition: Where an impartible-estate tenure dispute involves a conditional grant, a governmental power to remove an unfit holder, and successive recognition without fresh grants, those conditions do not create a life estate.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative recognition of a successor does not bar a civil court from determining succession where the recognition is not shown to result from the prescribed quasi-judicial inquiry into the competing claims.
material_facts: The Governor recognized a rival claimant as holder, but the order did not show that competing claims had been investigated or that the claimants had been heard.
There was no evidence that the order was made in exercise of the authority to determine succession under the grant and family custom.
The civil dispute concerned the claimants’ kinship and the family rules of succession.
issues.conclusion: The administrative order did not prevent the civil court from deciding the succession dispute.
issues.legal_principle: When exercising authority under the grant to determine succession, the Governor acts quasi-judicially and must decide the dispute after an inquiry consistent with natural justice and the family custom. The Court found no basis to treat the order in this case as an exercise of that authority and held that the administrative orders did not exclude the civil court’s jurisdiction to determine kinship.

rule.if: civil_succession_title_suit and administrative_recognition_order and (no_competing_claims_inquiry or claimants_not_heard or order_not_shown_to_apply_family_custom)

predicates.civil_succession_title_suit: A civil proceeding asks the court to determine competing claims to succession to an estate.
predicates.administrative_recognition_order: An administrative authority issued an order recognizing one claimant as successor or holder.
predicates.no_competing_claims_inquiry: The order was made without an inquiry into the competing succession claims.
predicates.claimants_not_heard: The competing claimants were not shown to have received an opportunity to be heard before the order.
predicates.order_not_shown_to_apply_family_custom: The order did not show that the authority decided the claims by applying the relevant family custom.

issues.definition: In a civil succession-title suit, an administrative recognition unsupported by an inquiry, a hearing, or an evident application of family custom does not prevent the civil court from determining succession.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation officer’s authority to determine proprietary rights in property vested in the State does not extend to deciding competing private claims to the compensation based on rival titles.
material_facts: Property vested in the State under the land-abolition legislation, and a compensation officer made a summary order concerning compensation for it.
The rival claimants asserted competing private titles to the property and the resulting compensation.
No timely civil suit was brought to set aside the compensation officer’s order.
issues.conclusion: The compensation officer’s order did not finally determine the competing private claims to compensation, and the civil court could decide which claimant was entitled to it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 14 and 35(7) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, distinguish the State’s liability to pay compensation from private disputes over entitlement to compensation. Section 14 permits summary determination of proprietary rights in the property as against the State; it does not confer jurisdiction to determine competing private claims founded on rival titles. Section 35(7) preserves the ability of another person to enforce rights against the person paid by due process of law.

rule.if: abolition_compensation_proceeding and compensation_officer_made_summary_order and competing_private_title_claims and claim_to_compensation_is_against_recipient

predicates.abolition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute arises in a proceeding to determine compensation after proprietary rights in property have vested in the State under an abolition scheme.
predicates.compensation_officer_made_summary_order: A compensation officer made a summary order concerning proprietary rights or compensation for the vested property.
predicates.competing_private_title_claims: Two or more private claimants assert competing titles to the property or the compensation derived from it.
predicates.claim_to_compensation_is_against_recipie: A claimant seeks to enforce an entitlement to compensation against the person who received or is to receive it.

issues.definition: When a compensation officer has made a summary order but private claimants assert rival titles and one seeks compensation from its recipient, the private compensation-title claim remains open for civil adjudication.
